 Statistical Analysis Plan

Sample Size Calculation
We tried to determine the rate of primary endpoint based on the randomized trials, but no randomized
trial has been conducted to evaluate outcomes of early surgery. Using a prospective registry data, we
recently reported that the estimated actuarial 6-year survival and cardiac mortality-free survival rates
were 98±1% and 100% in the early surgery group, 68±6% and 76±5% in the conventional treatment
group, respectively (p < 0.001) (9). Based on our prospective observational study, we estimated that a
sample size of 144 patients would provide 80% power to detect a significant difference with respect to
the primary end point at the 2-sided significance level of 0.05, assuming that the 4-year rate of a
composite end point (cardiac mortality or operative mortality) would be 16% in the conventional
treatment group and 2% in the early surgery group.

Analysis of primary and secondary end point
All primary and secondary endpoints will be analyzed on an intent-to-treat basis (all patients analyzed
as part of their assigned treatment group). For intent-to-treat analysis, all patients who sign the written
informed consent form and are randomized in the study will be included in the analysis, regardless of
whether or not the correct treatment is administered, or whether crossover occurs.
To analyze outcomes, estimates of cumulative event rates will be calculated by the Kaplan-Meier
method and compared employing the log-rank test. For Kaplan-Meier analysis, we will analyze all
clinical events by time to first event. Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals will be derived with
the use of the Cox proportional hazards model.
Subgroup analyses will be performed to determine whether the reduction in the primary end point after
early surgery is consistent in 2 prespecified subgroups of peak aortic velocity (<5 m/s vs. ≥5 m/s) and
etiology of AS (degenerative vs. non-degenerative), using Cox regression models with tests for
interaction.

Determination of Treatment Group Comparability
Baseline demographic and clinical variables will be summarized for each of the treatment groups. All
continuous variables will be summarized as mean and SDs, or medians (with 95% confidence intervals

Early Surgery for Asymptomatic Aortic Stenosis
Trial Procedures
Eligibility was determined after each patient un-
derwent a thorough evaluation of symptoms and
medical records and results of echocardiography
and exercise testing were reviewed. Details re-
garding echocardiography and exercise testing are
provided in the Supplementary Appendix, available
at NEJM.org. Patients were randomly assigned in
a 1:1 ratio to early surgery or conservative care
with the use of a Web-based interactive response
system. The assignment to each treatment group
was computer-generated and stratified according
to the participating center by means of a permuted-
block sequence with variable block size.
The protocol specified that patients assigned
to the early-surgery group should undergo aortic-
valve replacement within 2 months after random-
ization. Patients assigned to the conservative-care
group received treatment according to the ACC-
AHA guidelines,2,12 and they were referred for
surgery if they became symptomatic during fol-
low-up, if the left ventricular ejection fraction
decreased to less than 50%, or if the peak aortic
jet velocity increased each year by more than 0.5 m
per second on follow-up echocardiography. Details
regarding surgical procedures and patient follow-
up are provided in the Supplementary Appendix.
Trial End Points
The primary end point was a composite of op-
erative mortality or death from cardiovascular
causes during the follow-up period (continuing
until 4 years after the last patient was enrolled).
Prespecified secondary end points included death
from any cause, repeat aortic-valve surgery, clini-
cal thromboembolic events, and hospitalization
for heart failure during follow-up. Specific defi-
nitions of trial end points are provided in the
Supplementary Appendix.
Statistical Analysis
On the basis of our previous observational study,13
we estimated that a sample of 144 patients would
provide the trial with 80% power, at a two-sided
significance level of 0.05, to detect a significant
difference with respect to the primary end point,
assuming that the incidence of the primary end
point would be 16% in the conservative-care group
and 2% in the early-surgery group during a follow-
up period that continued until 4 years after the last
patient was enrolled. In calculating the sample size
by a log-rank survival power analysis, we also
assumed that an enrollment period of 2 years
would be needed to complete enrollment and that
the rate of loss to follow-up would be 10%.
Analyses were performed on an intention-to-
treat basis. Differences between the treatment
groups were evaluated with the use of Student's
t-test for continuous variables and Fisher's exact
test for categorical variables. Because random-
ization was stratified according to the partici-
pating center, we analyzed the end points with
the use of stratified Cox proportional-hazards re-
gression with Firth correction. Estimates of cu-
mulative incidences were calculated by the Kaplan-
Meier method and were compared with the use
of the log-rank test. For the Kaplan-Meier analy-
sis, we analyzed all clinical events according to
the time to the first event. Hazard ratios with
95% confidence intervals were derived with the
use of the stratified Cox proportional-hazards
model with Firth correction. The 95% confidence
intervals have not been adjusted for multiple com-
parisons, and therefore inferences drawn from
these intervals may not be reproducible.
For the primary end-point analysis, we also
performed a competing-risk analysis in which
death due to a cause other than a cardiovascular
cause was considered as a competing risk, and
hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were
calculated with the use of the method of Fine and
Gray. The cumulative incidences of the primary
end point were also compared between the treat-
ment groups with the use of Gray's test. Subgroup
analyses were performed to determine whether
the result of the primary end point was consistent
in two prespecified subgroups defined according
to peak aortic velocity and cause of aortic stenosis.
A per-protocol analysis of the primary end point
was also performed. All reported P values were
two-sided, and a P value of less than 0.05 was
considered to indicate statistical significance. We
used SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute), for
statistical analyses.
Results
Patients
From July 2010 through April 2015, a total of 273
asymptomatic patients with very severe aortic
stenosis were screened for participation in the
trial, and 145 were enrolled and were randomly

There was no operative mortality in the early- surgery group. Of the 72 patients assigned to conservative care, 53 patients (74%) underwent surgical aortic-valve replacement (52 patients) or transcatheter aortic- valve replacement (TAVR) (1 patient) during fol- low-up, mainly because of the development of symptoms (in 43 patients). Indications for aortic- valve replacement are listed in Table S2. Among these 53 patients, urgent surgery was performed in 9 patients (17%) who were admitted from the emergency department. There was no operative mortality among the patients who later underwent aortic-valve replacement; the median time from randomization to aortic-valve replacement was 700 days (interquartile range, 277 to 1469). Ad- ditional information on surgical procedures and results are provided in Table S3 and the Supple- mental Surgical Results section in the Supplemen- tary Appendix. The median follow-up was 6.2 years (interquar- tile range, 5.0 to 7.4) in the early-surgery group and 6.1 years (interquartile range, 4.5 to 7.3) in the conservative-care group. 6.2.7 Study Termination and Discontinuation

The enrollment period in this study is set at 2 and a half, but enrollment will be terminated when
enrollment of 6000 patients is completed. The safety evaluation committee would be held if the
difference of the definite stent thrombosis events between the 2 groups has got ≥ 5 cases.
If this study discontinued or early terminated, last contact date to the subject and the reasons of
the discontinuation will be recorded on the EDC. The reason of the early termination should be
recorded.
Patients who withdraw consent will be included in the safety analysis set and analyzed regarding
the clinical events associated with death (Figure 1)

7. ENDPOINTS

In this study, the following two co-primary endpoints and secondary endpoints will be evaluated
at 1 month (30 days) after enrollment as a primary analysis.

Primary and major secondary endpoints as well as death will be evaluated at 2 months (60 days)
after enrollment as a secondary analysis.

In the non-aspirin group, patients shall be switched to clopidogrel monotherapy after 1 month of
prasugrel monotherapy, and in the 1-month DAPT group, patients shall be switched to aspirin
monotherapy after the completion of DAPT with aspirin and prasugrel.

Exploratory analysis will be performed on primary and secondary endpoints at 1 year (365 days)
after stenting. Details of the analysis will be defined in the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP) and
the case-handling plan.

7.1
Co-primary Endpoints

The following co-primary endpoints will be evaluated at 1 month after enrollment. These
endpoints are also evaluated at 2 months (secondary analysis) and 12 months (exploratory
analysis) after enrollment.

1. Major bleeding endpoint (BARC 3 or 5 bleeding)12

comparing aspirin monotherapy with a P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy
following short or very short DAPT after PCI. Therefore, we sought
to compare aspirin with clopidogrel used as monotherapy beyond 1
month after PCI as the secondary analysis of the STOPDAPT-3 (the
ShorT and OPtimal Duration of Dual AntiPlatelet Therapy-3) rando
mized clinical trial.22
Methods
Study design, subjects, antiplatelet regimen,
and ethical issues
The STOPDAPT-3 was a prospective, multicentre, open-label, adjudicator-
blinded randomized clinical trial exploring an aspirin-free strategy after PCI.
The details for the study design and the primary results at 30 days were pre
viously reported.22 Briefly, the trial enrolled patients with acute coronary
syndrome (ACS) or those with HBR by the criteria of the Academic
Research Consortium irrespective of ACS who were planned for PCI
with DES with cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stents (Xience series,
Abbott Vascular).23 Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 fashion to
1-month aspirin-free prasugrel monotherapy or 1-month DAPT with aspirin
and prasugrel. At 1 month (between 30 and 59 days after the index PCI),
patients who had received DAPT were switched to aspirin (81-100 mg/
day) monotherapy (aspirin group), and patients who had received prasugrel
monotherapy were switched to clopidogrel (75 mg/day) monotherapy (clo
pidogrel group). Each group of patients were to continue the assigned anti
platelet monotherapy up to 1 year (between 335 and 394 days after the
index PCI). In this report, we compared the 1-year outcomes between
the aspirin and clopidogrel groups. The dates and details of discontinuation
(including both temporal and permanent), resuming, or change of aspirin,
P2Y12 inhibitors, and oral anticoagulation were collected in the database.
The mode of antiplatelet therapy was analysed on a daily basis derived
from the date of stopping or resuming the drug, and the adherence to the
protocol for antiplatelet monotherapy beyond 1 month was represented
by the status of antiplatelet therapy at 60 days from index PCI.
The planned staged PCI was to be performed within 3 months. When the
staged PCI was conducted before the primary analysis at 1 month, patients
should continue the allocated antiplatelet therapy without additional load
ing doses at the time of the staged PCI. There were no specific recommen
dations for antiplatelet therapy at the staged PCI performed after the
primary analysis at 1 month.
This 1-year analysis was conducted with the latest study database, updated
from the previously published 30-day analysis. The group assignments were
open to the patients and the attending physicians, but blinded to event adju
dicators, statisticians, the steering committee, and the sponsor (Abbott).
Complete lists of the study organization, participating centres, and investiga
tors are shown in the Supplementary data online, Appendix S1.
The patients provided written consent before entering catheterization
rooms. In emergent cases, verbal consent was permitted, but written consent
was taken from patients themselves or their legal representatives after the
stabilization of their conditions. Kyoto University Certified Review Board ap
proved the study protocol. This trial was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov
(NCT04609111).
Endpoints
The co-primary endpoints of the study were the cardiovascular endpoint
defined as a composite of death from cardiovascular cause, myocardial in
farction, definite stent thrombosis, or ischaemic stroke and the bleeding
endpoint defined as Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) 3
or 5.24 The major secondary endpoint was the composite of the co-
primary cardiovascular and bleeding endpoints representing net adverse
clinical events. The pre-specified secondary endpoints are listed in the
Supplementary data online, Appendix S1. Myocardial infarction and stent
thrombosis were adjudicated with the criteria of the Academic Research
Consortium, and stent thrombosis was applied to the stents implanted at
the index or staged procedures for the present study.25 Stroke was adjudi
cated when persistent symptoms over 24 h were confirmed, and transient
ischaemic attack was not regarded as a stroke event. Bleeding events were
also adjudicated with the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) and
the Global Utilization of Streptokinase and Tissue Plasminogen Activator
for Occluded Coronary Arteries trial (GUSTO) criteria.26,27 Other details
for the endpoints are provided in the Supplementary data online, Appendix
S1. Follow-up began from the time of randomization, and the time intervals
for the clinical events were indicated from the day of randomization.
The clinical events related to the co-primary endpoints were centrally ad
judicated with three or more event adjudicators blinded to the assigned
group based on the site reports in the electronic data capturing system. If
a conflict of judgment occurred, consensus was made with discussion.
Statistical analysis
The main analysis for the present report for the 1-year clinical outcomes
was the 30-day landmark analysis for the comparison between the aspirin
and clopidogrel monotherapy groups beyond 30 days and up to 1 year.
In the landmark analysis, we excluded those patients who had the endpoint
event of interest before 30 days, and thus, the number of patients included
in the landmark analysis was different according to the endpoint event of
interest. We also conducted the overall 1-year analysis evaluating the out
comes throughout 1 year. The study population for the main analysis was
the intention-to-treat (ITT) population. Per-protocol (PP) population in
the 1-year analysis was defined as the patients included in the PP analysis
at 30 days and receiving the assigned monotherapy with adherence to
the protocol at 60 days from the index PCI. Moreover, we conducted
the 60-day landmark analysis in the ITT and PP populations considering
the transition period of antiplatelet therapy. We also conducted the
30-day landmark analysis in patients without staged PCI. The power and
sample size calculation were performed, as previously reported, for the pri
mary analyses at 30 days.22 There was no pre-specified power calculation
for this secondary analysis of the 1-month landmark analysis.
Categorical variables were expressed as numbers and percentages, and
continuous variables were expressed as median [interquartile range
(IQR)]. The time-to-event curves were generated with the Kaplan-Meier
method censoring the patients without events at 365 days. We estimated
the incidence rates of the endpoints per 100 person-year from 30 days
to 1 year after PCI by the 30-day landmark analysis. The risks of the aspirin
group relative to the clopidogrel group for the endpoints were estimated
with the Cox's proportional hazards model and expressed as the hazard ra
tios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We performed the subgroup
analyses to evaluate the interaction between the subgroups and the risks of
the aspirin group relative to the clopidogrel group for the co-primary end
points. The adjustment of covariates was not performed because of the na
ture of the randomized clinical trial, and the imbalance was rare even after
excluding the patients with events within 30 days. The comparison was
made only with the superiority of one group to another. All reported
P-values were two sided, and P-values of <.05 were regarded as statistically
significant. The P-values and 95% CIs were not adjusted for multiplicity con
sidering the nature of the extended follow-up study of a previously re
ported trial. A physician (H.W.) and a statistician (T.M.) performed all
statistical analyses with the use of JMP version 16.1 and SAS version 9.4
(SAS Institute, Cary, North Carolina).
Results
Study population
Among the 6002 patients who were enrolled and received randomiza
tion in 72 PCI centres in Japan, the ITT population for the overall 1-year
analysis consisted of 5962 patients (2982 in the aspirin group and 2980
in the clopidogrel group) after excluding 40 patients who withdrew

consisted of 5833 patients (2920 in the aspirin group and 2913 in the
clopidogrel group) after excluding 129 patients who were dead by
30 days or lost to follow-up at 30 days (Figure 1). The PP population
for the overall 1-year analysis and for the 30-day landmark analysis con
sisted of 5023 patients and 4908 patients, respectively, after excluding
the non-adherent patients for antiplatelet therapy (Figure 1).
Baseline characteristics and antiplatelet
therapy
In the 5833 patients included in the 30-day landmark analysis, the median
age was 73 (IQR 64-80) years at baseline, and 23.4% were women. There
were 74.6% of patients who presented with ACS including 42.1% of pa
tients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (Table 1). The
prevalence of cardiogenic shock or ongoing heart failure was 4.0% and
17.8%, respectively. The prevalence of diabetes and severe chronic kidney
disease (estimated glomerular filtration rate < 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 or un
der maintenance dialysis) was 45.0% and 11.1%, respectively. Patients
with HBR accounted for 54.1%. Through the 1-year follow-up, planned
staged procedures were conducted in 20.7% of patients (maximum
four procedures including the initial PCI). Considering the characteristics
of all lesions treated in the index and staged PCI procedures, 24.3% of
patients received complex PCI by the definition of a previous report.28
The baseline characteristics were well balanced between the two groups
except for the higher prescription rate of proton pump inhibitors (PPI) in
the aspirin group than in the clopidogrel group (92.5% and 83.1%)
(Table 1). The proportion of prescribed PPI type is shown in the
Supplementary data online, Table S1. The baseline characteristics were
also well balanced between the two groups in the PP population for
the 30-day landmark analysis and in the ITT and PP population for the
overall 1-year analysis (see Supplementary data online, Tables S2-S4).
As for the adherence to the assigned antiplatelet regimen, 88.6% of
patients in the aspirin group received aspirin monotherapy and 87.8%
of patients in the clopidogrel group received clopidogrel monotherapy
at 60 days (Figure 2). At 1 year, 87.5% of patients in the aspirin group
and 87.2% of patients in the clopidogrel group continued the assigned
monotherapy (Figure 2). When the patients with clinical events were
censored, 91.1% of patients in the aspirin group and 90.3% of patients
in the clopidogrel group continued the assigned monotherapy at 1 year
(see Supplementary data online, Figure S1).
Endpoints
For the 30-day landmark analysis, follow-up was completed in 99.3%
both in the aspirin and clopidogrel groups. The incidence rate of the
co-primary cardiovascular endpoint from 30 days to 1 year after PCI
was not different between the two groups (aspirin group: 4.5 per
100 person-year and clopidogrel group: 4.5 per 100 person-year;
HR 1.00, 95% CI .77-1.30, P = .97) (Table 2; Figure 3A). The incidence
rate of the co-primary bleeding endpoint was also not different be
tween the two groups (aspirin group: 2.0 per 100 person-year and clo
pidogrel group: 1.9 per 100 person-year; HR 1.02, 95%CI, .69-1.52,
P = .92) (Table 2; Figure 3B). The incidence rate of definite or probable
stent thrombosis from 30 days to 1 year was not different between the
two groups (.2 and .2 per 100 person-year) without an obvious rise in
the Kaplan-Meier curves at 30 days after PCI (Table 2; Figure 3C). The
incidence rates of all-cause death; cardiovascular death; non-
cardiovascular death; myocardial infarction; stroke; BARC 2, 3, or 5
bleeding; gastrointestinal bleeding; and any coronary revascularization
were also not different between the two groups (Table 2). The results
of the 30-day landmark analysis in the PP population were fully consist
ent with those in the ITT population (see Supplementary data online,
Figure S2). Also, in the 60-day landmark analysis in the ITT and PP po
pulations, there were no significant differences in the co-primary end
points between the two groups (Supplementary data online, Figures S3
and S4). Moreover, even when excluding the patients who underwent
staged procedure, the results were fully consistent with those in the
entire study population (see Supplementary data online, Figure S5).
In the overall 1-year analysis, the cumulative 1-year incidence of the
co-primary cardiovascular endpoint was not different between the clo
pidogrel and aspirin groups (7.5% and 7.9%; HR .95, 95% CI .79-1.14,
P = .58) (see Supplementary data online, Table S5 and Figure S6A).
The cumulative 1-year incidence of the co-primary bleeding endpoint
was also not different between the two groups (6.5% and 6.1%;
HR 1.07, 95% CI .87-1.31, P = .53) (see Supplementary data online,
Table S5 and Figure S6B). The results of the overall 1-year analysis in
the PP population were fully consistent with those in the ITT popula
tion (see Supplementary data online, Figure S7).
Subgroup analyses
In the subgroup analyses, there were marginally significant treatment-by-
subgroup interactions in the complex PCI subgroups for the co-primary
cardiovascular endpoint (complex PCI: HR .62, 95% CI .36-1.05; non-
complex PCI: HR 1.18, 95% CI .87-1.60, P for interaction = .04) and in
the diabetes subgroups for the co-primary bleeding endpoint (diabetes:
HR 1.54, 95% CI .88-2.71; non-diabetes: HR .65, 95% CI .36-1.17, P
for interaction = .04). Otherwise, there were no treatment-by-subgroup
interactions for the co-primary bleeding and cardiovascular endpoints in
any subgroups including the subgroups stratified by PPI administration at
discharge (Figure 4).
Discussion
The key finding in the current study, which was the first study compar
ing aspirin monotherapy with clopidogrel monotherapy beyond 1
month after PCI with DES, was that aspirin monotherapy compared
with clopidogrel monotherapy was associated with similar cardiovascu
lar and bleeding outcomes beyond 1 month and up to 1 year after PCI
with DES (see Structured Graphical Abstract).
In the early phase of the endeavour to shorten the duration of
DAPT, several trials compared aspirin monotherapy following 3-6
months of DAPT with the conventional 12 months of DAPT with as
pirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor, mostly clopidogrel.3-9 These trials consist
ently demonstrated the lack of difference in cardiovascular events
between short and standard DAPT durations with a trend towards
reduction in bleeding events. In the late phase of the endeavour to fur
ther shorten the duration of DAPT, the use of more potent antiplate
let monotherapy was prioritized and a P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy
replaced aspirin monotherapy. Several recent clinical trials compared
a P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy (ticagrelor or clopidogrel) after 1-3
months of DAPT with the 12-15 months of DAPT with aspirin and
a P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor or clopidogrel).12-21 These trials consist
ently demonstrated a reduction of bleeding events without an increase
of cardiovascular events.12-21 Based on these observations, the cur
rent guidelines stated that shorter-duration DAPT would be reason
able with subsequent transition to a P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy to
reduce the risk of bleeding events in selected patients undergoing
PCI, although the default antiplatelet regimen recommended as

1.4. Supplementary statistical methods
1.4.1. Definition of rescue medication
Rescue medication was defined as any immunosuppressive medication that would be expected to materially
impact efficacy, regardless of whether the medication was used for IgAN. A blinded medical review of
concomitant therapy was performed to document which patients were defined as having rescue medication for
IgAN or prohibited immunosuppressive medications for non-IgAN indications, and therefore had some or all of
their data excluded from the relevant efficacy analyses. When the dose and duration of treatment received was
considered unlikely to have impacted all subsequent data, only data at specified visits were excluded. Initiation
of dialysis, renal transplantation, and renal-related death (although the latter did not occur) were also included
with rescue medication as reasons for exclusion of impacted data from the primary efficacy analyses.

1.4.2. Primary efficacy endpoint analysis: time-weighted average of eGFR over 2 years
Time-weighted average of eGFR measurements over 2 years were analysed using robust regression, having
multiply imputed any missing data first in three phases: an imputation, analysis, and pooling phase. Robust
regression was selected because previous eGFR data contained a small sub-population of patients having
extreme outlying data resulting from very rapid progression of disease. Robust regression avoids results being
unduly influenced by a small subset of patients with outlying data. Data at each individual time point were
log-transformed prior to analysis.

The first step of the imputation phase was to create data with a monotone data structure across time points
having imputed 20 datasets separately within each treatment arm. The number of burn-in iterations was set to
200, and observations were sampled every 200 iterations within the same chain for each imputed dataset. In the
second step of the imputation phase, data at each timepoint were multiply imputed using a regression method

4
sequentially imputing data across successive timepoints separately by treatment arm from each dataset imputed
in the first step. Having imputed any missing data, the time weighted average over 2 years was calculated for
each patient within each imputed dataset.

In the analysis phase, time weighted average eGFR data were analysed using robust regression with independent
variables of treatment and log-transformed baseline eGFR. M-estimation was used with Huber weights and a
cut-off value of 2, with the median method used to estimate the scale parameter. This approach means that
standardised residuals with an absolute value of ≤2, corresponding to the central 95% of the data if normally
distributed, have equal weight, and outlying data are weighted according to a pre-specified function, Wc(x),
which gives lower weights to the most outlying data where Wc(x)=min{1,c|x|} and x is the standardised
residual, corresponding to least square standardised residuals in the first iteration. Given that dependent variables
are categorical and inclusion criteria for the only continuous covariate, log-transformed baseline eGFR, prevents
this variable from having outlying values, M-estimation was deemed appropriate.

In the pooling phase, estimated treatment effects and associated standard errors from each imputation were
combined using Rubin's rules to provide an overall treatment effect, associated 95% confidence interval (CI),
and one-sided p value. For the purposes of presentation, data were back transformed and expressed as the mean
change from baseline in eGFR averaged over 2 years in each treatment arm and derived directly from the robust
regression analysis performed on the log scale by multiplying the baseline geometric mean eGFR, pooled across
treatment arms, with the ratio of geometric least-squares (LS) means within each arm minus 1. Diagnostic plots
for the analysis models and the residuals were checked. No evidence of violation of the modelling assumptions
was observed.

1.4.3. Primary supportive endpoint analysis: 2-year eGFR slope
The primary supportive analysis of 2-year eGFR total slope using a random coefficients analysis was planned
prior to unblinding Part A. However, in the presence of an acute effect this analysis method does not provide an
accurate estimate of the difference in the eGFR decline over 2 years as slope is not forced through baseline and,
as a result, it underestimates the magnitude of the treatment effect between the targeted-release formulation of
budesonide (Nefecon; Tarpeyo/Kinpeygo [Calliditas Therapeutics, Stockholm, Sweden]) and placebo.

Therefore, 2-year eGFR total slope was estimated as half of the between-arm difference in mean change from
baseline to 2 years derived from a robust regression analysis of the multiply imputed values of log-transformed
eGFR at 2 years used in the primary endpoint calculation. An analysis of 2-year eGFR total slope using a linear
spline mixed-effects analysis,7 with a fixed knot at 3 months, was also pre-specified prior to unblinding the full
study to provide a more accurate estimate of the magnitude of the 2-year eGFR total slope. This analysis method
was used in a previous meta-analysis by Inker et al.8

1.4.4. Secondary efficacy analyses
In the analysis of time to 30% eGFR reduction or kidney failure, the 30% reduction was to be confirmed at a
later time point. When a clinical event was confirmed, the time to the first reduction was used in the analysis.
The first eGFR reduction that was greater than 30% counted as a clinical event in the following situations:
•
If a later reduction was observed, but after at most one intervening occurrence where the eGFR had not
reduced by 30%, and the geometric mean reduction of these three values was reduced by greater than 30%;
•
The first reduction occurred at 24 months or the visit for the replicate eGFR sample, and there were no later
recordings of eGFR; and/or
•
The patient received dialysis, underwent renal transplantation, or died from a renal-related event after the
first reduction, but before a confirmation could be made.
Any patients who died from a renal-related event, or had dialysis for at least 1 month, kidney transplantation, or
kidney failure defined as a sustained eGFR <15 mL/min/1·73 m2 prior to a 30% reduction, were to be counted as
kidney failure events. Patients who were followed to 2 years without a confirmed 30% reduction, or with no 2-
year eGFR recording and no 30% reduction, or who received rescue medication prior to a 30% reduction were
censored in the analysis.

Because the use of rescue medication was likely to be higher among patients who were more rapidly
approaching a 30% reduction in eGFR, an analysis that censors at the point of rescue would result in informative
censoring and bias. Hence, to provide a more accurate estimate of the time to 30% reduction in eGFR, the
primary analyses used the Inverse Probability of Censoring Weights (IPCW) approach.9 Time varying stabilised
weights were derived using the following covariates: baseline values of log (baseline UPCR), log (baseline
eGFR), age, gender, race, geographical region, and diastolic blood pressure and time varying values of post-
baseline values of log (UPCR) and log (eGFR). Data were analysed using a weighted Cox model of time to 30%

5
reduction in eGFR in counting process format with covariates of treatment, log-baseline UPCR, log-baseline
eGFR, and geographical region. A supplementary analysis was performed that counted rescue medication as a
clinical event and analysed using an unweighted Cox model, including covariates of treatment, log-baseline
UPCR, log-baseline eGFR, and geographical region. Patients without an event were censored at the time of their
latest eGFR measurement. An additional post hoc analysis was also performed of time to 30% reduction in
eGFR using a standard Cox model and regardless of rescue medication. This was analysed using an unweighted
Cox model with the same set of baseline covariates. Post hoc analyses using the IPCW method to evaluate the
time to 30% reduction in eGFR for the subgroups of patients with UPCR <1.5 g/gram and UPCR ≥1.5 g/gram
were also performed. Proportional hazards assumptions were checked and confirmed.

The ratios of UPCR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio (UACR) compared with baseline, averaged over time
points between 12 and 24 months, were analysed using the Mixed-Effects Model for Repeated Measures with
separate visit terms for 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, and 24 months having log-transformed data. The treatment effects at 12,
18, and 24 months were given equal weight to obtain the geometric mean treatment effect averaged over these
time points. Baseline UPCR was included as a covariate and was calculated as the geometric mean of the two
baseline UPCR measurements and log-transformed prior to inclusion in the analysis model. The model also
included terms for treatment arm, visit, log (baseline)-by-visit, and visit-by-treatment arm interaction. A
common unstructured covariance structure was used to model the within-patient errors. The Kenward-Roger's
degrees-of-freedom adjustment was used. Restricted maximum likelihood was used to obtain parameter
estimates.

The analysis of geometric mean eGFR over 12 to 24 months (see Supplementary Table S6 for results) used the
same robust regression methodology that was applied to the primary time-weighted average of eGFR over 2
years, except that the visits at 12, 18, and 24 months were given equal weight. The time from the first dose of
study drug until receiving rescue medication (see Supplementary Table S7 for results) was analysed using a Cox
Regression Model. The proportion of patients receiving rescue treatment (see Supplementary Table S7 for
results) was a secondary endpoint of the study but was not subject to formal statistical analysis. There were no
differences observed between the groups in any of the domains of the Short Form 36 (SF-36) quality of life
assessment performed at 9 and 24 months. Data from the SF-36 quality of life assessment will be reported
separately.

1.4.5. Determination of the clinical relevance of the treatment effect on eGFR slope
The clinical relevance of the magnitude of the treatment benefit on 2-year eGFR total slope has been assessed by
comparison with a threshold derived from the meta-analysis by Inker et al.8 that defined the relationship between
eGFR slope and the composite clinical endpoint of kidney failure, eGFR <15 mL/min/1·73 m2 or sustained
doubling of serum creatinine.

Based on information provided by Inker et al.8 and given the precision with which eGFR total slope has been
estimated in this trial, it is calculated that an observed treatment effect of 1·23 mL/min/1·73 m2 per year mean
difference in 2-year eGFR total slope would confer >97·5% probability of an effect on the composite clinical
endpoint. This study-specific threshold was estimated using the slope, intercept, root mean-squared error, and
associated confidence intervals provided by Inker et al.8 for the relationship between 2-year eGFR total slope and
log (hazard ratio) for the composite clinical endpoint.

1.4.6. Hypothesis testing strategy
In order to provide strong control of the type I error rate of 2·5% one-sided across the study, the endpoints of
UPCR at 9 months in the first 199 randomised patients, time weighted average of eGFR over 2 years in the
overall study population, and 2-year eGFR slope in the overall study population were tested in an endpoint
hierarchy. This approach required the primary analysis of UPCR at 9 months to be tested at a one-sided
significance level of 0·02, in order to preserve 0·005 for the final analysis of 2-year eGFR in the overall study
population in case statistical significance was not achieved for UPCR. Because statistical significance at the
required threshold was achieved for the analysis of UPCR at 9 months, the primary time-weighted average of
eGFR over 2 years was tested at a one-sided significance level of 0·025. The primary supportive analysis of
2-year eGFR total slope was also included in the endpoint hierarchy. As statistical significance was achieved for
the time-weighted average of eGFR over 2 years at the one-sided significance level of 0·025, 2-year eGFR total
slope was also tested at a one-sided significance level of 0·025.

protocolSection.descriptionModule.briefSummary: "The overall aim of the study is to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of Nefecon 16 mg per day in the treatment of patients with primary IgAN (Immunoglobulin A nephropathy) at risk of progressing to end-stage renal disease (ESRD), despite maximum tolerated treatment with renin-angiotensin system (RAS) blockade using angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) or angiotensin II type I receptor blockers (ARBs)."
protocolSection.descriptionModule.detailedDescription: "This is a Phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter study to evaluate the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of oral Nefecon compared to matching placebo in patients with primary IgAN on a background of optimized RAS inhibitor therapy. The study will consist of 2 parts, Part A and Part B. Part A will include a 9 month blinded Treatment Period, and a 3-month Follow up Period. Part B of the study will consist of a 12-month observational Follow up Period; no study drug will be administered during Part B. Part A and B will be blinded. Safety will be monitored by an independent Data Safety Monitoring Board."

protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: ""
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "1. Female or male patients ≥18 years"
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "2. Biopsy-verified IgA nephropathy"
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "3. Stable dose of RAS inhibitor therapy (ACEIs and/or ARBs) at the maximum allowed dose or Maximum Tolerated Dose (MTD) according to the 2012 KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) guidelines"

protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: ""
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "1. Systemic diseases that may cause mesangial IgA deposition."
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "2. Patients who have undergone a kidney transplant."
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "3. Patients with acute or chronic infectious disease including hepatitis, tuberculosis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and chronic urinary tract infections."
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "4. Patients with liver cirrhosis, as assessed by the Investigator."
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "5. Patients with a diagnosis of type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus which is poorly controlled."
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "6. Patients with history of unstable angina, class III or IV congestive heart failure, and/or clinically significant arrhythmia, as judged by the Investigator;"
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "7. Patients with unacceptable blood pressure control defined as a blood pressure consistently above national guidelines for proteinuric renal disease, as assessed by the Investigator"
protocolSection.eligibilityModule.eligibilityCriteria: "8. Patients with diagnosed malignancy within the past 5 years."

Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) 4/6 inhibitors in combi-
nation with ET have improved outcomes for patients with
HRþ, HER2 ABC and have become a standard treatment
option on the basis of prolonged progression-free survival
(PFS).5,6 Abemaciclib is an oral, selective CDK4/6 inhibitor
with greater selectivity for CDK4 than CDK6, which, unlike
other currently approved CDK4/6 inhibitors, allows contin-
uous dosing due to less myelosuppression.7 Abemaciclib has
demonstrated efficacy as monotherapy and in combination
with AIs/fulvestrant in ABC in the MONARCH trials2,8-10 and
also in combination with ET in node-positive, high-risk early
breast cancer (EBC) in the monarchE trial,11 which has led to
regulatory approvals in both the metastatic and adjuvant
settings.
In the absence of cure, improvement in overall survival
(OS) remains an important goal for patients with ABC. In
MONARCH 2, the addition of abemaciclib to fulvestrant
significantly improved both PFS and OS in patients with
HRþ, HER2 ABC with disease progression on prior ET.8,12
MONARCH 3 is a phase III trial evaluating abemaciclib in
combination with a nonsteroidal aromatase inhibitor (NSAI)
in postmenopausal women with HRþ, HER2 ABC who
have not received prior systemic therapy in the advanced
setting. The primary objective was previously met with the
results showing significantly prolonged PFS with the addi-
tion of abemaciclib versus placebo to NSAI [median, 28.2
months versus 14.8 months; hazard ratio, 0.540; 95% con-
fidence interval (CI) 0.418-0.698; P 1⁄4 0.000002].2 At the last
interim OS analysis (5.8-year follow-up), a numerically
favorable median OS difference of 12.6 months was
observed (hazard ratio, 0.754; 95% CI 0.584-0.974; P 1⁄4
0.0301, non-significant).13 Here, we report the results of the
prespecified final OS analysis of MONARCH 3.
METHODS
Procedures
MONARCH 3 is a global, randomized, double-blind, placebo-
controlled, phase III study evaluating abemaciclib with an
NSAI versus placebo with an NSAI in postmenopausal
women with HRþ, HER2 ABC who have not received prior
systemic therapy in the advanced setting. The NSAI selected
was anastrozole or letrozole per physician's choice. Prior ET
in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting was permitted if the
patient had a disease-free interval >12 months from the
completion of ET. This study was conducted in 158 centers
in 22 countries.
Eligible patients were randomized in a 2 : 1 ratio to
receive abemaciclib or placebo (150 mg twice daily
continuous schedule) plus either 1 mg anastrozole or 2.5 mg
letrozole daily. Cycles were 28 days. Stratification factors
included metastatic site (visceral, bone only, other) and
prior (neo)adjuvant ET (AI, other, none). The presence of
visceral disease refers to lung, liver, pleural, peritoneal, or
adrenal gland involvement at the time of randomization.
Additional study details were previously reported.10
This study was funded by the sponsor, Eli Lilly and Com-
pany, and designed together with the steering committee.
The study was carried out in compliance with the Declara-
tion of Helsinki. The study protocol and amendments were
approved by the relevant ethical and institutional review
boards and all patients gave written informed consent.
Patients
Women 18 years of age with locally tested HRþ, HER2
breast
cancer,
postmenopausal
status,
locoregionally
recurrent disease not amenable to resection or radiation
therapy with curative intent, or metastatic disease were
eligible. Patients must have had measurable disease or non-
measurable bone-only disease, as defined by RECIST v1.1, in
addition to adequate organ function and an Eastern Coop-
erative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS)
score of 1.
Patients with visceral crisis, lymphangitic spread, lep-
tomeningeal carcinomatosis, inflammatory breast cancer, or
evidence or history of central nervous system metastasis
were excluded. Prior CDK4/6 inhibitor or systemic therapy
for advanced disease was not permitted.

In each participating centre, patients were randomly
assigned by a web-based application (MRCC IWRS

without blocking or stratification methods. Patients who
met all the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion
criteria were randomly assigned in consecutive order
to either the clopidogrel group (75 mg once daily) or
aspirin group (100 mg once daily) in a ratio of 1:1
(figure 1). This study used a web-based electronic case
report form with the Pharmaco-epidemiology and
Clinical Trial Application X (PhactaX), which was
developed by the MRCC. When patients previously
using potent P2Y12 inhibitors were randomly assigned to
the clopidogrel group, clopidogrel 600 mg loading was
recommended for ticagrelor users, while prasugrel
users switched to clopidogrel 75 mg without a loading
dose. Participants and study investigators were not
masked to the assigned group.
Procedures
Participants received either clopidogrel (75 mg once
daily) or aspirin (100 mg once daily) orally. Clinical
follow-up was scheduled at 12 months and 24 months
(each with a window of plus or minus 3 months). Any
additional visits were at the discretion of attending
physicians. On each visit, active surveillance was done
for any adverse clinical events, along with the assessment
of adherence to the study drug.
Outcomes
The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause death,
non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, readmission due
to acute coronary syndrome, and major bleeding
complications during the 24-month follow-up period.
Major bleeding was defined as Bleeding Academic
Research Consortium (BARC) type bleeding of least 3.
The individual components of the primary endpoint,
revascularisation, and minor gastrointestinal complica
tions were analysed as secondary endpoints at 24 months.
Interim analysis was not planned and was not done
during the follow-up duration. Post-hoc secondary com
posite endpoints, including the thrombotic composite
endpoint (defined as cardiac death, non-fatal myocardial
infarction, ischaemic stroke, readmission due to acute
coronary syndrome, and definite or probable stent
thrombosis) and any bleeding (defined as BARC type ≥2
bleeding), were analysed. Detailed definitions of each
clinical event are described in the appendix (pp 13-18).
The vital status of all patients was cross-checked through
the National Health Insurance Service system of South
Korea and the South Korea National Statistics System.
The definite cause of death was confirmed by the
recorded data classified by the International Classification
of Disease, 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes.
Additionally, all source data were checked for at least
